ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory risk-based screening of all directors, officers, shareholders, and significant controllers against the Public Safety Canada terrorist entity list, Criminal Code Part II.1 terrorist listings, Global Affairs Canada consolidated sanctions list, UN Security Council consolidated lists, OFAC SDN list (where USD clearing is used), and all regulations under the Special Economic Measures Act; Politically Exposed Persons (PEP) enhanced due diligence is required under FINTRAC guidelines for non-Canadian PEPs and all PEPs in higher-risk jurisdictions; independent AML compliance officer and suspicious transaction reporting obligations apply from the moment the entity engages in financial activity.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Registraire des entreprises du Québec (Système d'analyse des rapports d'analyse - SARA) at registreentreprises.gouv.qc.ca; federal counterpart NUANS (nuans.com) administered by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (Corporations Canada)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Under the Charter of the French Language (CQLR c. C-11), corporate names and constitutive filings in Quebec must be drafted in French; a version in another language may be added only where the name is a recognized trademark or a statutory exception applies. Official transliteration must follow general French Latin-script rules and comply with the Registraire's rules on distinctive, descriptive, and generic elements of a corporate name.
prohibited_and_sensitive_tokens: CUSTOMS BROKER (permitted only upon proof of CBSA licence under the Customs Act)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Upon refusal of a corporate name by the Registraire des entreprises du Québec under the Act respecting the legal publicity of enterprises (CQLR c. P-44.1), the applicant may correct and re-file the name electronically; within 30 days of an effective refusal, a written request for administrative review may be submitted to the Registraire; a further judicial appeal lies before the Court of Québec within 30 days of the review decision. Where a federal name reservation under the CBCA is revoked, the applicant may appeal to the Director of Corporations Canada within 30 days accompanied by the statutory filing fee.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: NOT PERMISSIBLE as sole solution. Under the Quebec Business Corporations Act (CQLR c. S-31.1), the registered office (siège social) must be a physical address in Quebec where books and records are kept and legal notices may be served. The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) also requires licensed customs brokers under the Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations (SOR/86-1075) to maintain an operational place of business; a virtual office serves only as a mail-forwarding complement and never as the statutory registered office.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: ELEVATED (~65% probability within the first 12 months of operation). CBSA conducts routine and unannounced licence-verification inspections, and FINTRAC may perform on-site AML/CFT compliance examinations. This risk is substantially higher than the generic corporate average because ISIC 5229 customs brokerage is a licensed, record-intensive activity subject to continuous regulatory monitoring.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Québec Business Corporations Act (CQLR c S-31.1), sections 16-27 (incorporation by articles), 28-33 (share issuance), 35-38 (registered office), and 53-60 (directors and officers)
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Registraire des entreprises du Québec (Québec Business Registry), in cooperation with the Gouvernement du Québec's Services Québec online portal
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Articles of Incorporation (Statuts de constitution) filed with form AR-51/C-A2 via the Registraire des entreprises
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No minimum paid-up capital is prescribed under the QBCA; nominal consideration for founders' shares is acceptable, and no escrow account is required for corporate formation.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED: That the corporation accept the share subscriptions set forth in the attached subscription list, and that directors issue the corresponding shares in accordance with section 28 of the Québec Business Corporations Act. FURTHER RESOLVED: That the registered office be established at [specific address in Québec], and that [custodian name] be appointed to maintain the corporate records and share register. FURTHER RESOLVED: That [President name] be appointed President, [Secretary name] Secretary, and [Treasurer name] Treasurer, each to serve at pleasure until successors are elected. FURTHER RESOLVED: That all pre-incorporation actions taken on behalf of the corporation are hereby ratified and confirmed.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registraire des entreprises du Québec (via Services Québec online portal, onlineservices.servicesquebec.gouv.qc.ca)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit a company name search request using a proposed business corporate name (in French or bilingual) for the customs brokerage house. If the name is not distinctive enough, modify and resubmit. Obtain the 'Rapport de recherche de nom/Attestation de réservation' if required. Note: For Quebec, the corporate name must be in compliance with the Charter of the French Language.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is refused or queried, file an alternative name request within 10 business days or apply to the Director of the Registraire for a formal review under Section 19 QBCA.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Drafting and Filing Articles of Incorporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registraire des entreprises du Québec (via Service Québec's corporate tele-formation portal)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Complete form AR-51/C-A2 'Articles of Incorporation' indicating the corporation's name, share structure (including share classes if more than one), restrictions on share transfers if any, initial registered office address, and declaration of directors. File the articles electronically, pay the required filing fee, and ensure at least one director or incorporator signs the electronic form. Keep the signed copy as part of corporate records.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registraire issues a notice of deficiency or refusal, correct the specified articles (e.g., add a French version of the corporate name, clarify share classes) and re-file. Administrative refusal may be challenged via judicial review before the Superior Court of Quebec within 30 days of notice.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registraire des entreprises du Québec / Corporate's own registered office record keeper
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: After issuance of the Certificate of Incorporation (Certificat de constitution), prepare and maintain the company's minute book, including the first board resolution, share register, register of directors, and registered office records. File the 'Declaration of Immatriculation' (form AR-1) if the corporation is also required to obtain a Québec enterprise number (NEQ). Update the register within 30 days of any change to address or officers.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the declaration is late or incomplete, file a remedy and pay the administrative late fee; the Registraire may also reinstate a dissolved or struck-off corporation if application is made within 10 years and taxes are settled.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Register for Tax and Payroll Accounts
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Revenu Québec (www.revenuquebec.ca) and Canada Revenue Agency (www.canada.ca/cra)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Obtain a Québec enterprise number (NEQ) from Revenu Québec and a federal Business Number (BN/RT) from the CRA. Register for Quebec QST, GST/HST, corporate income tax, and employer payroll accounts. If the customs brokerage house employs personnel, set up source deductions, workers' compensation (CNESST) account, and registrer for Quebec's Commission des normes, de l'équité, de la santé et de la sécurité du travail (CNESST) occupational health and safety declarations.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If registration is delayed, apply for provisional accounts with the tax authorities; late-filing penalties may be waived if a written request for voluntary disclosure is made under the CRA's Voluntary Disclosures Program or Revenu Québec's equivalent.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Open Corporate Bank Account and Seal
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Canadian chartered bank or credit union (e.g., secured through banking partner)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Provide the corporate minute book, certificate of incorporation, NEQ confirmation, board resolution appointing authorized bank signing officers, and identity documents of all officers/directors. The bank will conduct AML/KYC due diligence. Funds may be deposited for initial working capital; no escrow is required.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the bank refuses due to insufficient corporate documents, obtain a certified copy of the articles and a fresh board resolution confirming the same authorized signatories, and re-submit.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) – Customs Licensing Unit, in cooperation with the Office de la protection du consommateur (professional licensing, if applicable for customs consulting practices in Quebec)
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: Customs Broker Licence (issued under the Customs Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (2nd Supp.) and the Customs Broker Licensing Regulations) / Quebec consumer protection permit (if advising the public directly)

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: Ministère de l'Environnement, de la Lutte contre les changements climatiques, de la Faune et des Parcs (MELCCFP) – Gouvernement du Québec
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt (low-risk professional office activity; no industrial manufacturing or pollutant-generating process)
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: N/A for typical office operations; must comply with municipal wastewater bylaws and workplace air quality standards under the Regulation respecting industrial and commercial establishments (CQLR c Q-2, r. 10). Hazardous waste (if any) must be disposed of through a permitted transfer station per the Regulation respecting the recovery and elimination of contaminated soils.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Fire safety clearance is required from the local fire prevention service (e.g., Ville de Montréal Fire Prevention Division) based on occupancy type; the office must meet the Quebec Building Code (CQLR c B-1.1, r. 1) for structural load and egress. Occupational health and safety clearance is provided by the CNESST after the employer registers for coverage and implements a workplace health and safety program. A registered training certificate for all customs brokerage employees is also necessary to obtain CBSA security (bearer) clearance and an electronic clerical clearance known as 'CBSA ECI'.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada (ARC) — federal GST/HST and corporate income tax, portal: CRA My Business Account (https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/e-services/cra-login-services.html); Revenu Québec — Quebec Sales Tax (QST) and Quebec corporate income tax, portal: Revenu Québec CLIC (https://www.revenuquebec.ca/en/on-line-services/).
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: Step 1: Register extra-provincially in Quebec by obtaining a Quebec Enterprise Number (NEQ) from the Registraire des entreprises du Québec within 60 days of commencing business activities. Step 2: Obtain a federal 9-digit Business Number (BN) from CRA by filing RC4601 (Application for a Business Number) or through the CRA BizPortal; non-resident corporations must designate a Canadian agent/representative where required. Step 3: Activate the 'RT' GST/HST program account with CRA; registration is compulsory once the corporation ceases to be a small supplier, i.e., worldwide taxable supplies (including zero-rated exports) exceed CAD 30,000 in the four preceding calendar quarters or in the current quarter; voluntary registration is prudent to claim input tax credits. Step 4: Register for QST with Revenu Québec by filing the online registration application in CLIC; the QST account references the federal BN plus the 'RQ' prefix; Quebec applies the same CAD 30,000 small-supplier threshold. Step 5: Obtain a customs broker licence from the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) under Section 9(1)(a) of the Customs Act, including a corporate security bond of at least CAD 25,000, professional indemnity insurance, and designation of a licensed individual broker. Step 6: Onboard into the CBSA Assessment and Revenue Management (CARM) Client Portal for mandatory electronic release, accounting, and duty/tax payment through ACH or wire.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Corporation is classified as a taxable Canadian corporation under the Income Tax Act (Part I) and the Quebec Taxation Act (Part IV); no US-style check-the-box election exists — entity classification is determined by corporate law. Available elections include: (1) ETA s. 156 election for closely related corporations (90% or more common ownership) to zero-rate intercorporate taxable supplies; (2) ETA s. 273 joint venture election; (3) GST/HST Quick Method election (ETA s. 227) for small registrants; (4) ITA s. 85 rollover election to transfer property into the corporation at agreed amounts; (5) ETA streamlined accounting for non-resident registrants; (6) Quebec mirror elections under the QST Act and Taxation Act; (7) capital dividend account election (ITA s. 83) for tax-paid corporate surplus distributions.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax (GST/HST) plus Quebec Sales Tax (QST); administered federally by CRA and in Quebec by Revenu Québec; customs duties and border taxes administered by CBSA through CARM.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 — worldwide taxable supplies (including zero-rated export supplies) in the four preceding calendar quarters or the current quarter; ETA s. 148(1); Quebec QST applies the identical threshold.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada does not operate a real-time tax-authority clearance or digital-stamping e-invoicing regime; CRA permits electronic GST/HST invoices meeting the information requirements of ETA s. 169 and ETA Regs. s. 238 provided data integrity is preserved. Mandatory electronic filing of GST/HST returns applies once annual taxable supplies exceed CAD 1.5 million (GST/HST NETFILE or approved EDI). For customs brokers, CBSA CARM mandates fully electronic release and accounting via the CARM Client Portal, EDI/API integration, automated declaration processing, electronic posting of exporter/importer statements, and ACH/wire duty-and-tax settlement; legacy B3 paper accounting is obsolete for licensed brokers.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Customs brokerage services supplied to a non-resident in respect of goods exported from Canada qualify for 0% GST/HST under Schedule VI, Part V, s. 7 ETA (services in respect of tangible personal property exported by the supplier or delivered to a common carrier for export), and are similarly zero-rated for QST under the Quebec Sales Tax Act where the supply is made to a non-resident and the service relates to exported goods. International freight-forwarding and transportation services tied to a destination outside Canada also qualify. The broker must charge 0% at point of sale and retain contemporaneous evidence that (i) the service recipient is a non-resident, (ii) the goods were physically exported from Canada, and (iii) the service is attributable to those goods; input tax credits (ITCs/IVRTs) on related expenses remain fully claimable.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration (B13A) filed electronically via CBSA Canadian Export Reporting System (CES)
CBSA Commercial Invoice / customs invoice showing foreign purchaser, exporter, routing, and value
Bill of Lading (ocean B/L, airway bill, or CMR truckwaybill endorsed for export)
Inward Remittance Certificate (bank-transfer/SWIFT evidence of foreign-currency payment settlement)
CBSA CARM account statement demonstrating zero-rated accounting lines
ACI eManifest export control record or CBSA-approved transit documentation
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA and Revenu Québec may reassess within four years of the reporting period under normal reassessment rules, and without limitation where misrepresentation, neglect, or fraud is established. Failure to substantiate zero-rating triggers reassessment at 5% GST plus 9.975% QST on the gross service consideration, with statutory interest and compound arrears interest. Gross-negligence penalties under ETA s. 280.1 and QSTA equivalent equal the greater of CAD 250 and 25% of the net tax evaded; false statements or omissions carry an additional 50% penalty for a second occurrence. Deliberate evasion is prosecutable under ETA s. 327 and Criminal Code s. 380, with fines up to 200% of the tax sought to be evaded and imprisonment up to five years. Licensed customs brokers face CBSA administrative monetary penalties (AMPS) up to CAD 25,000 per violation, joint and several liability for duties/taxes incorrectly released under Customs Act s. 17-18, and licence suspension or revocation for systemic non-compliance. Any foreign exchange proceeds retained beyond the customary 180-day benchmark without documented commercial justification are treated by CRA as unrepatriated export revenue, exposing the broker to transfer-pricing adjustments under ITA s. 247 and potential reassessment of the zero-rating claim.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada) as the central monetary authority; Canada maintains no dedicated foreign-exchange control administration. Effective regulatory authority for cross-border banking and FX compliance is distributed among OSFI (Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions) for bank prudential conduct, FINTRAC (Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada) for AML/ATF transaction surveillance, Payments Canada for clearing membership, the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) for customs duty and broker licence administration, and Global Affairs Canada / Innovation, Science and Economic Development (ISED) for Investment Canada Act foreign-investment administration.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The Canadian dollar is fully convertible on both current and capital accounts; Canada satisfies IMF Article VIII obligations and imposes no exchange controls, prior-approval licensing, or profit-remittance authorisation for dividends, interest, fees, or capital repatriation. Practical remittance hurdles are tax and reporting based: (i) outbound dividends and interest to non-resident shareholders attract Part XIII withholding tax (Canadian statutory rate 25%, reduced typically to 5%-15% under an applicable income tax treaty); (ii) non-resident inter-company payments must withstand transfer-pricing scrutiny under Income Tax Act section 247, and shareholder debt must respect the thin-capitalisation ratio of 1.5:1 debt-to-equity (ITA s.18(4)) plus the Excessive Interest and Financing Expenses Limitation (EIFEL) imposed on net interest expense exceeding C$250,000 annually, with a 30% EBITDA cap; (iii) all wire transfers, large cash transactions, and cross-border electronic funds transfers above C$10,000 are FINTRAC-reportable; (iv) brokerage fees charged to Canadian clients attract GST at 5% and Quebec QST at 9.975%, while fees supplied to non-resident clients in respect of documented export movements may be zero-rated under the Excise Tax Act and the Quebec QST Act.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Canada imposes no statutory export-proceeds surrender, no mandatory conversion ratio, and no fixed timeline for converting foreign-currency receipts into Canadian dollars; exporters and licensed customs brokers may freely retain USD, EUR, CNY, or any convertible currency. For a customs brokerage house, the analogous surrender and remittance obligations are: (i) import duties and taxes collected from clients are trust funds owing to His Majesty and must be settled with the Receiver General for Canada through the CBSA Assessment and Revenue Management (CARM) system on the prescribed due date, normally the date of release where funds are cleared, or under a CBSA-approved deferred payment arrangement underwritten by a customs surety bond (Form B6-1), with maximum deferral of approximately 30 days (monthly plan) or 45 days on a semi-annual bond; (ii) no duty deferral is available to an unlicensed entity or a broker whose surety bond has lapsed; (iii) GST/HST and QST collected on brokerage fees are remitted to CRA and Revenu Québec on the normal monthly or quarterly filing cycles; (iv) office cash receipts above C$10,000 trigger a FINTRAC Large Cash Transaction Report filed within 15 calendar days.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Quebec Annual Declaration (Déclaration annuelle) — REQ registry update
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Registraire des entreprises du Québec (Quebec Enterprise Registrar)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Annually no later than June 15 for an enterprise registered with REQ on or before January 1; for an enterprise registered during the current year, within 60 days after the anniversary of registration.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing administrative penalty of CAD 100 or more; failure to file for two consecutive years may result in administrative dissolution by the Registrar, loss of legal personality, and inability to obtain attestations from the entreprise registrar.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Federal Annual Return under the Canada Business Corporations Act (CBCA)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada / Corporations Canada
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 days after the corporation's anniversary date or the annual return date assigned by Corporations Canada.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing penalties up to CAD 250; failure to file for two consecutive years may trigger administrative dissolution under the CBCA, after which the corporation can be revived only on filing of all outstanding returns and payment of arrears.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) — Calgary Tax Centre
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: No later than six months after the corporation's fiscal year-end; date of tax payment is due no later than two months after year-end for a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC), or three months for a non-CCPC.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing penalty equal to 5% of unpaid tax plus 1% per full month, up to 12 months; provision of book reserve reliefs may be denied after 18 months; directors may be subject to liability for unremitted withholdings.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: No later than six months after the corporation's fiscal year-end; instalment and balance-due deadlines follow the Quebec Taxation Act rules.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing penalty of 5% of unpaid Quebec tax plus 1% per month up to 12 months; interest at the prescribed rate is compounded daily on arrears; persistent non-filing may lead to estimated assessments and collection action.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Customs Broker Licence Annual Surety and Material Change Confirmation
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) — Customs Licensing and Registration Directorate
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Annually on or before the licence anniversary; material changes in directors, principal officers, financial standing, or surety insurance must be reported to CBSA within 30 days of occurrence.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to maintain valid surety security may result in suspension or revocation of the customs broker licence; operating without a valid licence is an offence under the Customs Act and subjects the operator to summary conviction fines and loss of broker privileges.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: The Quebec Business Corporations Act (QBCA) does not impose a size-based audit threshold; a private business corporation must appoint an auditor unless all shareholders consent in writing by unanimous resolution to dispense with an audit for the fiscal year. If the corporation is a reporting issuer, if any shareholder holding at least 5% of the voting shares opposes the waiver, or if the directors are unable to provide unaudited statements that satisfy applicable law, a statutory audit remains mandatory.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: Canadian accounting standards as set out in the CPA Canada Handbook; Part I IFRS applies to publicly accountable enterprises, while Part II Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises (ASPE) is adopted by the Corporation for private corporate reporting. Revenu Québec and CRA accept financial statements prepared under IFRS or ASPE provided they present fairly the results and financial position in accordance with the applicable standard.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: Under the Act respecting the legal publicity of enterprises, the Corporation must maintain an up-to-date register of persons with significant control. Any share transfer that changes significant ownership must be recorded in the register within 15 days of the Corporation receiving reliable notice. The annual declaration filed with the Registraire des entreprises du Québec must reflect the current persons with significant control, and directors are responsible for certifying the accuracy of such information on each annual filing.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Persons with Significant Control

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 1,500 – 4,500 per year for a single-entity private corporation

corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: Small Business Deduction (SBD): federal rate reduced from 15% to 9% and Quebec rate reduced from 11.5% to 3.2% for a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) on up to CAD 500,000 of active business income annually; refundable SR&ED investment tax credits available; no general statutory tax holiday regime.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return filed electronically via CRA Internet File Transfer / EFILE through the Canada Revenue Agency Business Number portal.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual; instalments are generally required monthly where the corporation expects to owe tax in excess of applicable thresholds.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: T2 must be filed no later than six months after the fiscal period end; balance-due tax is payable no later than three months after year-end for qualifying CCPCs and two months after year-end for other corporations.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Entry bears net of business, property, capital gains and adjustments; non-capital loss carryforwards are deducted here.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Compute Canadian-source taxable income attributable to a permanent establishment in Canada pursuant to section 115 and applicable treaty rules.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Schedule 1 – Federal Tax on Taxable Income
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Tax on taxable income is calculated at 15% federal general rate, with provincial abatement applied where applicable; CCPCs claim SBD here.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident-controlled corporation normally cannot claim SBD; the 15% general rate applies to Canadian PE income subject to treaty-based rate limitations.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Claims federal investment tax credits, foreign-tax credits, and other non-refundable credits.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Foreign tax credits may be claimed for income tax paid to the home country if that income is also taxed by Canada.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Reports accounting policies, reconciliations and out-of-country payer/supplier schedules for bearer transactions.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Ensure all non-resident payments are traced for Part XIII withholding and treaty compliance.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: ITA s.162(1): 5% of unpaid tax plus 1% per complete month up to 12 months; repeated failure penalty of 10% under s.162(2); s.161 interest compounded daily on unpaid balances; gross negligence penalty of 50% under s.163(2); criminal prosecution possible.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: Revenu Québec Form CO-17 – Corporation Income Tax Return, filed electronically via Revenu Québec's 'Mon dossier d'entreprise' online portal.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual; instalments are due if estimated Quebec corporate tax exceeds CAD 1,000.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: CO-17 must be filed within six months of fiscal year-end; balance-due date is three months after year-end for qualifying CCPCs and two months for others, subject to applicable instalment credits.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Starts from federal taxable income after re-attribution and Quebec-specific adjustments.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report only Quebec-source income attributable to a Quebec permanent establishment.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Apply Quebec general corporate rate of 11.5%; eligible CCPCs apply 3.2% rate on first CAD 500,000 of active business income.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident corporations use the general 11.5% rate; reduced rate is unavailable.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Allocates taxable income between Quebec and other jurisdictions based on gross revenue and wage factors.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Only Quebec PE income appears in the numerator; corroborate with T2 PE allocation.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Quebec innovation, export and other refundable or non-refundable credits.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Claim only to the extent that credits are attributable to Quebec-source active business income.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Revenu Québec late-filing penalty: 5% of unpaid tax plus 0.7% per month up to 12 months; prescribed interest accrues daily; directors are jointly and severally liable for unremitted Quebec taxes under the Taxation Act.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% Part XIII withholding tax on dividends and deemed dividends paid to non-resident shareholders, including dividends arising from paid-up capital reduction and profit capitalization; the Quebec share of withholding is collected federally under the Canada–Quebec administration agreement.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To invoke a reduced treaty rate, the non-resident shareholder must provide the Canadian payer with a completed CRA Form NR301 (or NR302/NR303 for specific payment categories) and a certificate of residence / Tax Residence Certificate from the home-jurisdiction tax authority. The payer then withholds at the treaty rate; if tax has been over-withheld, the non-resident must file a refund application with CRA and Revenu Québec, attaching the treaty evidence and T2-type reconciliation documents.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory Part XIII rate for non-resident interest and royalties is 25%. Interest paid to an arm's-length non-resident creditor is generally exempt from withholding under the arm's-length interest exception in s.212(3); otherwise DTA rates for interest commonly range from 0% to 15%, with US treaty arm's-length interest often exempt. Royalties for patents, trade-marks and copyrights are domestically subject to 25%, with DTA reductions typically to 0% or 10% depending on the IP class and country of residence; Canada-US treaty may exempt copyright royalties and provide 0% on industrial royalties under specified conditions.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: CRA requires contemporaneous transfer-pricing documentation when the aggregate value of non-arm's-length cross-border transactions with related non-residents exceeds CAD 1,000,000 in a taxation year (CRA administrative materiality threshold; no strict statutory threshold is codified, but absence of documentation shifts the audit burden to the taxpayer and may attract penalties).
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada's federal and provincial tax systems do not apply named 'Economic Substance Regulations' of the UAE type; however, the GAAR (ITA s.245) and Quebec's anti-avoidance rule (Quebec Taxation Act s.1079.1) will recharacterize transactions that lack genuine economic substance or that are primarily tax-motivated. A customs brokerage house must also satisfy federal CBSA licensing requirements, demonstrating an active commercial presence, office premises, staff and actual brokerage operations.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Willful false reporting of brokerage commission revenue, suppression of cash receipts, or deliberate overstatement of customs clearance expenses in T2 or CO-17 filings; fabricating invoices for freight and customs services.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Civil gross negligence penalty of 50% of understated tax (ITA s.163(2)); criminal conviction under ITA s.239(1) for tax evasion attracts fines ranging from 50% to 200% of tax evaded and up to 5 years imprisonment; Revenu Québec equivalent penalties apply under the Quebec Taxation Act.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who authorized false filings are jointly and severally liable for unremitted tax amounts; the corporate veil can be pierced in civil fraud claims; director assets may be seized, and criminal conviction may include imprisonment.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Interposing a Canadian entity with no employees, no physical office, no operating risk, and no independent judgment solely to divert customs brokerage profit to a low-tax foreign affiliate.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: CRA and Revenu Québec invoke GAAR to deny the tax benefit, adjust taxable income, and levy interest and penalties; conduit arrangements may create deemed dividends subject to 25% Part XIII withholding; false ownership declarations trigger s.163 penalties.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors can be assessed personally if assets were transferred out of the corporation at amounts less than fair value (ITA s.160); courts may disregard separate legal personality and order direct directors' liability for unpaid corporate taxes and restitution.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Charging intercompany markups or management fees to the Canadian customs brokerage entity that are not consistent with the transactional net margin that an independent broker would earn (e.g., a 5% cost-plus on low-risk distribution while Canadian entity bears full customs liability).
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: ITA s.247(2) adjusts profits to arm's-length levels; s.247(3) imposes a 10% penalty on the net adjustment where documentation is missing and gross misstatement exists; QST and federal interest accrue on reassessed balances.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors are not ordinarily personally assessed for transfer pricing penalties absent fraud, but they are personally liable for unremitted Part XIII or source withholding taxes; failure to document may expose directors to director-liability proceedings for taxes owed by the company.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Submitting false customs declarations through the Automated Broker Interface (ACH), misclassifying goods to evade duty, operating an unlicensed customs brokerage in Canada, laundering proceeds through freight transactions, or failing to file Suspicious Transaction Reports (STR) with FINTRAC.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Customs Act penalties up to CAD 25,000 per false declaration, seizure/forfeiture of goods, CBSA licence revocation; FINTRAC administrative monetary penalties up to CAD 2,000,000 for Anti-Money Laundering (AML) failures; criminal liability under the Criminal Code of Canada for smuggling and laundering, with serious fines and imprisonment.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and licensed customs brokers are exposed to personal Criminal Code prosecution; convictions may trigger asset freezing, travel bans as bail conditions, and heavy personal fines; the corporate veil is pierceable where the company is used as an instrument for customs fraud or laundering.
